## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="a11-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<!-- a11-ideas:start (written from the data file by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Boundary</dt><dd>On site, a solar farm emits 0 g per kWh; from cradle to grave, about 43 g, mostly from making the panels.</dd>
<dt>One boundary</dt><dd>Gas at its stack (389 g) against solar from cradle to grave (43 g) is unfair; on one boundary it is 486 against 43.</dd>
<dt>Water</dt><dd>Withdrawn is not consumed: once-through cooling takes 11,380 gal per MWh and consumes 100.</dd>
<dt>Land</dt><dd>Counting the land between moves gas from 4.1 to 19.0 m² per MWh a year, past solar.</dd>
<dt>A load</dt><dd>A data center's indirect water, 1,194 gal per MWh it uses, is about 12 times its own cooling water (U.S., 2023).</dd>
<dt>Two questions</dt><dd>A new solar farm's share is about 43 g per kWh; what changes depends on what it replaces.</dd>
<dt>Drought</dt><dd>In EIA's drought case, hydropower falls from 15% to 8% of California's summer generation and gas rises from 45% to 50%.</dd>
</dl>
<!-- a11-ideas:end -->
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Medians, ranges and harmonization</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **Medians of published studies.** NREL screened about 3,000 life-cycle studies and kept fewer than 15% (2021).
- **Medians need not add.** Gas's phases add to 461 g per kWh, its total median is 486 g.
- **Harmonized.** Re-running studies on common assumptions narrows the spread: crystalline-silicon panels 45 g per kWh (middle half 39 to 49), combined-cycle plants 450 g (420 to 480). Both from the papers' abstracts.
- **What moves a solar number most.** Sunshine, panel life and efficiency, and the grid that powered the factory.
- **What moves a gas number most.** The plant's efficiency, and methane leaked on the way from the well. The harmonized gas studies count methane at its 100-year warming effect (Heath et al., 2014).

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>Shared burdens and system expansion</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **Two products, one plant.** When a plant sells both power and heat, its burden must be split (by energy, by value) or the study is widened to include what the second product replaces: system expansion (ISO 14044).
- **Attributional and consequential, by name.** IPCC AR6 Working Group III, Annex III (2022): attributional studies use average data for a product's own impacts; consequential studies widen the boundary to the effects of a change, and depend more on their assumptions.
- **In a model.** What responds to a change is an output of a dispatch or planning model: [A10](a10-emissions-questions.html) asks it for a day, [M6](m06-carbon-in-models.html) over years.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this lesson leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>Any one real plant: its sunshine, gas field, river and grid.</li>
<li>Harms other than climate, water and land: air pollution, toxicity, wildlife.</li>
<li>Mines and factories' land and water, and a data center's servers and buildings.</li>
<li>Where water is scarce: a gallon consumed in a desert counts the same here as one by a full river.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="a11-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="zero" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A solar farm has no carbon footprint.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. On site it burns nothing, but from cradle to grave it is about 43 g CO₂e per kWh (NREL's median), mostly from making the panels.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="withdraw" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A plant that withdraws more water consumes more.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Once-through cooling withdraws 11,380 gallons per MWh and consumes 100; a cooling tower withdraws 255 and consumes 205 (medians).</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="dcwater" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Most of a data center's water is the water it cools with.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth, for the U.S. average in 2023: 99 gallons per MWh on site against 1,194 at the power plants and reservoirs that make its electricity (Berkeley Lab).</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="a11">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="cool" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">A gas plant with a cooling tower makes 1,000 MWh. At the medians, how much water does its cooling consume?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">255,000 gallons</li><li data-value="b">205,000 gallons</li><li data-value="c">11,380,000 gallons</li><li data-value="d">205 gallons</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>205,000 gallons: 205 gallons per MWh × 1,000 MWh.</p><p>255,000 is what it withdraws; 11,380,000 would be the withdrawal of once-through cooling.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```

<li>USGS. <a href="https://www.usgs.gov/mission-areas/water-resources/science/thermoelectric-power-water-use">Thermoelectric Power Water Use</a>, 2020 estimates (Galanter et al., 2023); page read 6 November 2026.</li>
<li>EIA, Today in Energy: <a href="https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=56820">power-sector water efficiency</a> (14 June 2023: combined-cycle plants withdrew 2,803 gallons per MWh on average in 2021); <a href="https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=36773">dry cooling</a> (29 August 2018); <a href="https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=51839">hydropower in the 2021 drought</a> (30 March 2022).</li>
<li>EIA. <a href="https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/steo/special/supplements/2022/2022_sp_02.pdf">Short-Term Energy Outlook Supplement: Drought Effects on California Electricity Generation and Western Power Markets</a>, May 2022, Summary.</li>

</ul>
